strengths: The paper addresses a practically motivated and clearly articulated problem: zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) without anomalous samples, masks, or fine-tuning, which is a meaningful step beyond the few-shot fine-tuning paradigm (FSAG) that dominates prior work.

The proposed framework is technically coherent: delta-denoising attribution (accumulating per-step discrepancies between two synchronized diffusion branches), normal-reference guided initialization, mask-guided latent inpainting in the late denoising stage, and token-level prompt refinement with spatially biased cross-attention combine into a sensible, well-described pipeline (Fig. 2 and Algorithm 1).

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: quantitative generation-quality comparison (IS, IC-LPIPS) against five baselines across 15 MVTec categories, a downstream anomaly-detection evaluation with a consistent protocol, qualitative comparisons including unseen categories, and ablations of all three main modules (Table 3, Figs. 4-5).
The method achieves the best average results among zero-shot methods in both generation quality and downstream detection, demonstrating the practical utility of the synthesized data.

The paper is clearly written, the method section includes sufficient detail for reproduction, the authors commit to releasing code, and the limitations section is honest about restricted controllability and difficulty with abstract/logical defects.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core localization idea: deriving an edit mask by contrasting diffusion predictions from two prompts under a shared schedule is essentially the DiffEdit mechanism [9], which the authors cite but do not clearly delineate their contribution against. The delta-accumulation, prompt refinement, and attention biasing appear incremental relative to DiffEdit-style masking plus standard latent inpainting; a direct comparison to a DiffEdit-based anomaly-generation baseline is missing and would substantially clarify the contribution.

The central claim of 'strong localization fidelity' is not quantitatively supported: no pixel-level mask evaluation against ground-truth anomaly masks is reported in the main text (Table 1 reports IS and IC-LPIPS only, and downstream detection is an indirect proxy). Given that mask precision is a key selling point versus AnomalyAny, direct mask-quality metrics (e.g., AUROC/AP of generated masks vs. GT defect regions) are needed.

The evaluation relies heavily on MVTec AD; results on the other datasets are deferred to the appendix and not verifiable from the manuscript. Results on even one additional domain in the main paper would strengthen the cross-category generalization claim.

The method has many manually chosen hyperparameters (t_start, mid-stage threshold 0.6, final threshold 0.35, gamma = 0.3, refinement steps, step size, beta, eta) with limited sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness across domains and reproducibility of the reported numbers.

Inception Score is a questionable and dated fidelity/diversity metric for industrial images; perceptual or MLLM-based quality judgments (acknowledged by the authors as a future need) would be more convincing.

Efficiency and compute cost are not reported: the method runs two synchronized diffusion branches for T=100 steps, applies SAM, and performs per-image token-level prompt optimization via gradient descent, so per-image wall-clock time and comparison with AnomalyAny's inference cost should be given, especially given the paper's motivation of rapid data bootstrapping.

Downstream gains over AnomalyAny are moderate on average (AUC_i 84.7 vs 77.6; AUC_p 84.9 vs 83.3) and inconsistent per category (e.g., clearly worse on screw, zipper, bottle pixel-level metrics in Table 2), which tempers the significance of the improvement; variance/seeds across the generation and training procedures are not discussed.

The zero-shot framing deserves scrutiny: the method depends on SAM for the early foreground mask and requires a hand-crafted anomaly type prompt per category, which partially shifts the annotation burden rather than removing it.

strengths: Clear problem framing: the shift from few-shot anomaly generation (FSAG) to zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) is well motivated, and the paper correctly identifies the tension between annotation cost/overfitting and the need for realistic, well-localized synthetic defects.

The core idea of delta-denoising attribution — accumulating per-step denoising discrepancies between two prompt-conditioned diffusion branches — is an interesting and coherent way to derive image-specific anomaly masks without anomalous training data, and it is described with sufficient algorithmic detail (Alg. 1) for reproducibility.

The pipeline is fully training-free, combining normal-reference guided initialization, two-stage mask-guided latent inpainting, token-level prompt refinement, and spatially biased cross-attention; this practicality is valuable for industrial settings where defects are rare.

Experiments include quantitative generation metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS), downstream detection benchmarks against both FSAG and ZSAG baselines, and ablations covering all three proposed modules with both visualization and downstream detection evidence.
The paper includes an honest limitations section acknowledging constrained controllability, surface-level defects only, and weak evaluation protocols for ZSAG.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The method is largely a recombination of well-established techniques: prompt-difference delta masks are closely related to DiffEdit [9], partial-noise guided initialization is essentially SDEdit [25], and the inpainting formulation is standard latent blending. The token-level refinement and attention biasing are incremental variants of Attend-and-Excite-style ideas. The contribution reads as an application/engineering integration rather than a new algorithmic insight, and the paper does not analyze *why* delta-denoising attribution is superior to a single-step DiffEdit-style delta mask or cross-attention thresholding (e.g., the AnomalyAny baseline).

Evaluation is thin for the claims made. The main paper reports only MVTec AD; results on 'other datasets are provided in the appendix', which is insufficient to substantiate the claimed 'cross-category generalization across industrial and other domains'. Only 15 object categories with repetitive textures are covered, and the qualitative figures mostly reuse the same smooth-texture categories (hazelnut, wood, capsule).

The quantitative metrics are weak proxies for the central claims. IS and IC-LPIPS do not measure defect realism or fidelity to the requested anomaly type; no human study or MLM-based realism/faithfulness evaluation is provided, even though the paper itself lists the absence of MLLM-based assessment as a limitation. The claim of 'high realism' therefore rests largely on qualitative inspection.

Fairness and interpretability of the downstream comparison (Tab. 2) is questionable. Few-shot baselines are acknowledged to use test-set anomalies and masks (data leakage), yet are placed in the same table without a leakage-controlled protocol; conversely, the ZSAG comparison against AnomalyAny controls the source normal image, which is itself a special protocol that is not analyzed. The large per-category variance (e.g., AP_p of 0.2 on hazelnut vs 76.6 on AnoGen, 28.4 on bottle) suggests brittleness that is not investigated.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters and design choices is not examined: t_start, threshold values (0.6, 0.35), gamma=0.3, refinement step size, number of refinement iterations, and dependence on SAM mask quality are all fixed by default without sensitivity analysis. Since SAM provides the foreground prior and the anomaly prompt provides the semantic prior, failure cases where SAM misses the defect-bearing region or the prompt mismatch is diffuse are not characterized.

Controllability — one of the two stated desiderata of AG in the introduction — is evaluated only through a small qualitative figure (Fig. 5) with hand-picked prompt variants; no quantitative controllability or mask-quality (e.g., IoU against real defect masks) metric is reported, unlike what the mask-precision claims would require.

The 'training-free' claim needs qualification: token-level prompt refinement performs gradient updates on text embeddings per image, adding non-trivial inference cost and per-image optimization that is not timed or compared against AnomalyAny's inference speed, despite the intro criticizing that method for slow inference.
Writing is generally clear but the paper overclaims in places (e.g., 'great generalization', 'consistent gains') relative to the mixed per-category results and the single-dataset evidence.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: the paper targets zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) without anomalous samples or fine-tuning, which addresses a genuine practical limitation of few-shot anomaly generation (annotation scarcity, category overfitting, cross-category transfer).

The core idea is elegant and well-articulated: delta-denoising attribution accumulates per-step denoising discrepancies between two synchronized diffusion branches driven by a minimal prompt pair, tying anomaly localization directly to the model's own denoising dynamics rather than coarse attention maps.

The method is described as training-free and the components (normal-reference guided initialization, latent inpainting, token-level prompt refinement, spatially-biased cross-attention) are clearly formalized with equations and an inference algorithm, supporting reproducibility; code release is promised.

Comprehensive experimental protocol: generation quality (IS, IC-LIPS), downstream detection utility (image- and pixel-level AUROC/AP with a U-Net trained only on synthetic data), qualitative comparisons across MVTec categories plus unseen categories, and module-level ablations with both visualizations (Fig. 4) and quantitative detection metrics (Table 3).

Honest framing of comparisons: the paper acknowledges the ZSAG setting differs from FSAG, notes possible data leakage in FSAG baselines, and includes a genuine limitations section (limited evaluation protocols, coarse controllability, difficulty with abstract/logical defects).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior diffusion-editing work: contrasting two branches under a shared schedule to obtain a mask closely parallels DiffEdit [9], and the remaining components are compositions of known techniques (SDEdit-style partial-noise initialization, latent inpainting, Attend-and-Excite-style prompt refinement, cross-attention biasing). The paper would benefit from a more explicit differentiation and ablation against a DiffEdit-style baseline.

The claim of being fully training-free and zero-shot is somewhat weakened by the dependence on SAM [22] to provide the foreground mask M_fg at inference, an external model whose quality directly conditions the pipeline; the sensitivity of results to SAM mask quality is not analyzed.

Mask/localization quality of the generated anomalies is not quantitatively evaluated against ground-truth anomaly masks (e.g., pixel-level AUC of generated masks vs. real defect masks); Table 1 evaluates realism/diversity but not mask precision, despite mask precision being a central claim (Fig. 1 positions mask precision as a key advantage).

Main quantitative results are confined to MVTec AD; results on other datasets are deferred to the appendix and not visible in the main paper, limiting assessment of cross-domain generalization claims. Some thresholds and hyperparameters (t_mid = T/2, thresholds 0.6/0.35, γ = 0.3, refinement step size) are fixed without sensitivity analysis.

Downstream comparison fairness is debatable: generating 100 anomalies per category from a single normal source image per category isolates generation effects but may not reflect the diversity achievable by baselines, and per-category results in Table 2 show several categories where AnoAny or FSAG methods remain superior (e.g., screw, capsule), which deserves more discussion.

IS and IC-LIPS are coarse proxies for realism/diversity in the anomaly-generation context; no human or MLLM-based perceptual study is included, which the authors themselves note as a limitation of the field.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically motivated and well-defined problem: zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) that requires neither real anomalous samples nor fine-tuning, which is a sensible extension beyond few-shot anomaly generation (FSAG).

The technical framework is coherent and clearly described: contrasting two synchronized diffusion branches with a minimal prompt pair (in the spirit of DiffEdit) to accumulate per-step denoising deltas into an anomaly mask, followed by mask-guided latent inpainting, normal-reference-guided initialization, token-level prompt refinement, and spatially biased cross-attention. Each component is motivated and formally specified (Eqs. 1-13, Algorithm 1).

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: generation quality (IS, IC-LPIPS) on MVTec AD (Tab. 1), downstream detection on both MVTec AD and VisA (Tabs. 2-3), comparison against both ZSAG and FSAG baselines (App. C.1), module ablations with both qualitative and quantitative evidence (Fig. 5, Tab. 4), threshold sensitivity (Tab. 6), SAM-dependence analysis (C.2), and runtime/memory comparisons (C.3).

The method is shown to be backbone-agnostic (SD1.5 and FLUX.1-dev), which supports the claim of generality, and it is roughly 6x faster with much lower memory than the closest ZSAG baseline AnomalyAny.

The appendix contains an unusually honest and thoughtful critical discussion of the limitations of current AG evaluation protocols (App. D), and the limitations section acknowledges real shortcomings (controllability, structural/surface-level defects only).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty relative to prior work: the core localization mechanism (contrasting two prompt branches under a shared schedule and thresholding accumulated differences) is essentially DiffEdit [9] repurposed for anomaly generation. The added components (prompt refinement, attention biasing) are individually well-established techniques (cf. Attend-and-Excite, blended latent diffusion). The delta-denoising attribution framing packages known ideas, though the two-stage mask accumulation and inpainting schedule is a non-trivial adaptation for the ZSAG setting.

Potential test-set leakage in hyperparameter selection: the default mask thresholds (T1=0.6, T2=0.35) are explicitly chosen based on downstream detection performance evaluated on the MVTec AD test split (Tab. 6, Sec. 4.4). Although the authors argue the result is robust, tuning pipeline hyperparameters against held-out test metrics weakens the claim of strict zero-shot evaluation.

High variance and some anomalous results in downstream detection undermine the reliability of the gains: e.g., on MVTec AD the SD1.5 variant underperforms AnomalyAny on several categories (capsule AUCi 54.9 vs 59.4; transistor), and the FLUX variant reports screw AUCi/AUCp of 100.0/46.6 with APp of 0.2, which is inconsistent and unexplained. Mean-level superiority is modest (e.g., 84.7 vs 84.4 AUCi for SD1.5 vs AnoStyler).

Mask quality, which the paper itself identifies as central to the contribution (precise masks are a headline claim and a critique of AnomalyAny), is never directly measured; there is no mask-alignment metric or quantitative mask evaluation, only qualitative figures and indirect downstream evidence. This is a notable gap given the claimed mask-precision advantage.

Some evaluation choices are debatable: IS is a weak fidelity proxy for industrial defect imagery, and IC-LPIPS comparisons may be confounded as the authors themselves argue in App. D - yet these metrics are still used as primary evidence in Tab. 1. Additionally, the comparison to FSAG methods (App. C.1) uses different evaluation splits/protocols and the authors acknowledge the comparison is confounded.

Clarity and presentation issues: the code-availability statement in the abstract is incomplete (empty URL); Fig. 3 shows a 'Not Applicable' marker for baselines without explanation; several ablation results are only qualitative in the main text; and some claims (e.g., 'consistent gains in downstream detection') overstate results that are mixed at the category level.

The paper does not discuss how sensitive the method is to the choice of anomaly-type vocabulary (crack/scratch/hole), which implicitly encodes domain knowledge; only limited discussion appears in App. B.2, and no systematic study of prompt sensitivity is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely practical problem: anomaly generation when no real anomalous samples exist, avoiding the few-shot fine-tuning paradox that weakens FSAG methods. The motivation is clearly articulated.

The method is fully specified and reproducible in principle: Algorithm 1, hyperparameters (T=100, thresholds 0.6/0.35, beta=4, eta=4), and prompt templates are provided, and the appendix gives extended implementation details.

The framework is empirically demonstrated to transfer across backbones (SD1.5 to FLUX.1-dev) without architecture-specific tuning, which supports the model-agnostic claim, and the efficiency comparison (10.25 s/img vs. 67.4 s/img for AnomalyAny) is a useful practical result.

Experiments cover both MVTec AD and VisA with image-level and pixel-level metrics, and ablations (module removal, threshold sensitivity, SAM dependence) are provided; the appendix candidly discusses weaknesses of existing ZSAG evaluation protocols.

Limitations are discussed honestly, including restricted controllability and the difficulty of abstract/logical defects, and the acknowledgment that FSAG comparisons involve partial data leakage is fair.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core delta-denoising attribution is essentially DiffEdit [9] (contrast two diffusion branches under a shared schedule to derive an edit mask) applied to anomaly images. The paper cites DiffEdit and admits inspiration, but the remaining components—latent inpainting (blended latent diffusion), prompt embedding refinement (Attend-and-Excite style), and attention biasing—are largely re-combinations of known editing techniques. The genuinely new contribution is thin for a general algorithm contribution.

Quantitative gains are marginal and oversold. In Table 1 the IS improvement over AnoStyler is 2.05 vs. 2.04, and the text claims 'consistently higher IS and IC-LPIPS' while several categories are clearly below baselines (leather, tile, zipper, grid, capsule vs. AnomalyAny/AnoStyler). Downstream detection gains are also modest (e.g., SD1.5 means 84.7/91.3/84.9/30.5 vs. AnoStyler 84.4/91.5/78.2/30.2).

Inconsistent or anomalous results are not explained: e.g., screw in Table 2 achieves 100.0/100.0 AUCi/APi with FLUX yet pixel-level AUCp collapses to 46.6 with APp of 0.2; capsule drops sharply under DeltaDeno (SD1.5) relative to baselines. These patterns suggest fragility or possible protocol artifacts that the paper does not analyze.

The chosen default threshold configuration is not the best in the paper's own sensitivity analysis (Table 6): T1=0.4/T2=0.35 gives 86.3/92.6/84.1/35.3 vs. the default 0.6/0.35 at 84.7/91.3/84.9/30.5, and 0.6/0.60 gives higher image-level scores. The justification for the default is unclear and raises concerns about result cherry-picking or at least under-tuning.

Evaluation relies on weak, questionable proxies: IS is poorly calibrated for industrial defect imagery, IC-LPIPS is acknowledged in Appendix D to be ill-suited to the zero-shot setting, and the downstream U-Net protocol (100 synthetic anomalies from a single normal image) entangles generator quality with detector behavior. The appendix's critique of these protocols is thoughtful, but the paper does not then offer a stronger alternative, so the headline claims rest on the protocols it itself undermines.

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat undermined by reliance on SAM for the foreground prior in the default configuration (the SAM-free ablation drops APp from 30.5 to 29.2 and image-level AUROC from 84.7 to 83.3), plus iterative prompt-embedding optimization—per-image gradient steps are a form of test-time optimization.

Comparison fairness issues: AnoStyler is cited as AAAI'26, i.e., concurrent work, and reported numbers for it and AnomalyAny may not be reproduced under a unified protocol; the paper's own Appendix D.2 argues that differing detection backbones confound comparisons, yet Tables 2 and 3 inherit exactly this confound.
No code or data is currently available ('Code will be made publicly available'), which weakens verifiability given the many sensitive thresholds and design choices.
Fig. 6 labeling is confusing (the '(a/e) w/o Lanom' caption placement), and qualitative figures are small, making the central realism claims hard to verify from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: zero-shot anomaly generation (ZSAG) without anomalous samples, fine-tuning, or pixel-accurate masks. The motivation from industrial scarcity and distribution shift is convincing and clearly argued.

The core idea of accumulating per-step denoising discrepancies between two prompt-conditioned diffusion branches into an image-specific anomaly attribution map is a clean, elegant formulation. The two-stage design (coarse early-stage mask + inpainted late-stage refinement) is coherent and well-specified, with a clear Algorithm 1.

Experiments are comprehensive for the setting: generation quality (IS, IC-LPIPS) on MVTec AD, downstream detection on both MVTec AD and VisA against strong recent ZSAG baselines (AnomalyAny, AnoStyler), comparison against FSAG upper-bound methods (Tab. 5), module and threshold ablations (Tab. 4, 6), a SAM-dependence ablation, and runtime/memory analysis showing a large efficiency advantage over AnomalyAny.
The method demonstrates backbone transferability (SD 1.5 to FLUX.1-dev) without tuning, which supports the claim that the framework is model-agnostic rather than tuned to one generator.

The appendix is unusually thorough and honest: it critically discusses limitations of existing evaluation protocols for ZSAG (Sec. D), acknowledges that downstream detection conflates generator quality with detector choice, and clearly states remaining limitations (Sec. Limitations). This transparency strengthens the scientific case.
The quantitative ablation (Tab. 4) shows each component (inpainting, attention biasing, prompt refinement) contributes measurably, not just qualitatively.
weaknesses: Originality is the main concern. The core localization mechanism is essentially DiffEdit's prompt-contrast mask derivation applied to anomaly generation, and the surrounding components are established techniques: token-level embedding refinement resembles Attend-and-Excite/Textual Inversion-style optimization, spatial attention biasing resembles Prompt-to-Prompt-style attention control, and latent inpainting with a normal reference follows blended latent diffusion/SDEdit practice. The combination is well-engineered and tailored to ZSAG, but no single element is conceptually new; the paper would benefit from sharper positioning of what is genuinely novel beyond DiffEdit for defects.

Per-category results are highly uneven, and some are difficult to interpret. E.g., in Table 2, FLUX gives screw AUC_i=100/AP_i=100 but AUC_p=46.6/AP_p=0.2, an extreme inversion suggesting the detector may learn to classify image-level normality from the single-source normal image rather than segment defects. Similarly, cable and capsule results are inconsistent across backbones. The paper does not analyze these failure modes; a discussion or sanity check (e.g., detectors trained on real-only positives) would materially strengthen the downstream claims.

The two-stage thresholding scheme (T1=0.6, T2=0.35) is reported as category-sensitive, and Table 6 shows wide metric swings across thresholds (e.g., AUC_p from 69.1 to 84.9). This suggests the fixed default may be tuned to MVTec AD and questions robustness on truly unseen domains, despite the 'dataset-agnostic' claim; only qualitative evidence is given for unseen categories (Fig. 3 last row, Internet images).

The 'training-free' claim needs qualification: token-level prompt refinement performs gradient descent updates on prompt embeddings (Eq. 12) per image, and SAM is invoked as an external model. These are fine, but the terminology conflates 'no fine-tuning of the generator' with 'no training at all'; the claim should be stated more precisely.

The downstream evaluation protocol, while following AnomalyAny for comparability, evaluates each category-specific U-Net only on a held-out portion of the test set with 100 synthetic anomalies from a single normal image. Variance over this small setup (seeds, choice of the single normal image) is not reported; error bars or multi-seed results would improve confidence, particularly given single-image-driven results in the 50-60% AUC_i range for some categories.

Attribution of gains is partly confounded: the FLUX results outperform baselines, but the baselines use SD-based or non-diffusion generators, so some reported advantage stems from backbone strength rather than the proposed attribution mechanism itself. A same-backbone ablation against DiffEdit-style localization without the prompt refinement/biasing additions would isolate the contribution better.

Reproducibility: code is promised but not yet released; some constants (thresholds, beta, eta, gamma) are given, which helps, but the description prompt construction ('or similar variants') is under-specified.
